question: What was the total dollar value of the external debt stock of MICs in 2025 when excluding China?
answer: The total dollar value of the external debt stock of MICs in 2025, excluding China, was $6.9 trillion [worldbank-idr-2026_p31_para_001].

When China is excluded, the cumulative external debt stock of MICs increased
at a much faster pace—by 9.1 percent in 2025, to $6.9 trillion in 2025. An
increase of that magnitude has not been seen since 2017 and was concentrated
among the 10 largest LMIC borrowers other than China. 1 These borrowers
account for 59.5 percent of all LMIC external debt. Half of them recorded
double-digit increases in their borrowing levels in 2025, led by a 29.2 percent
increase in Ukraine’s debt stock, to $250.3 billion, following continued and
unprecedented support from the Group of Seven countries and multilateral
creditors.

The change in debt stock was
driven by net debt inflows of $423.5 billion, a more than twofold increase from
2024, as well as by some debt forgiveness and the upward accounting effect of
US dollar depreciation. During the first half of 2025, the US dollar experienced
its biggest depreciation against other currencies in more than five decades, and
the increase in new debt flows went largely to middle-income countries (MICs),
predominantly because of continued support from multilateral creditors and a
rebound in lending from private creditors.

Movements in the value
of the US dollar against other global currencies affect the value of LMICs’ debt,
and the size of these fluctuations in 2025 had important implications for LMICs,
particularly those with large dollar-denominated external debt portfolios. For this
subset of countries following a flexible exchange rate regime, dollar-denominated
debt became cheaper to service.
Additionally, in this publication, the US dollar is used as the common currency by
convention to measure all external borrowing of LMICs, which has implications
over time. As the US dollar depreciated in 2025 against the euro, the British pound,
the Chinese yuan, and many other currencies, the debt stock denominated in those
currencies increased when converted to US dollars.

question: In the Key Takeaways, did debt burdens ease or rise in IDA-eligible countries in 2025?
answer: Debt burdens eased in IDA-eligible countries in 2025, with their external debt-to-income ratio declining slightly from 42.1 percent to 41.2 percent [worldbank-idr-2026_p21_para_001].

• Debt burdens eased in IDA-eligible countries but rose elsewhere. Despite
a sharp increase in borrowing, IDA-eligible countries saw their external
debt burdens decline slightly in 2025. Their debt-to-income ratio fell
from 42.1 percent to 41.2 percent, as economic growth outpaced debt
accumulation, and some countries benefited from debt restructuring. The
picture was different for other developing economies. Excluding China,
LMICs saw their debt-to-income ratio rise to 34.5 percent, as debt grew faster
than national income.
• Other financial flows to LMICs continue to diverge, with negative
consequences. Foreign direct investment (FDI) and personal remittances to
LMICs continued to diverge in 2025, a trend that has been accelerating over
two decades.

This growing divide
carries long-term implications for growth, because FDI builds productive
capacity whereas remittances primarily support households and remain less
connected to productive investment.
In addition to the release of the 2025 external debt data from the International
Debt Statistics database, this edition of the International Debt Report provides
• An analysis of macroeconomic conditions and risks LMICs face amid
changing global financial and trade conditions and what these shifts imply for
these countries’ debt burdens and vulnerabilities;
• A discussion of how rising debt service burdens, elevated financing needs, and
changing financing patterns are constraining fiscal space and intensifying debt
and rollover risks, as well as the policy priorities for strengthening resilience;
• An analysis of how elevated debt burdens appear to be associated with
adverse changes in healthy diet unaffordability in LMICs during periods of
global stress and of potential underlying mechanisms, including food import
reliance and diversification; and
• An update on progress of the debt transparency agenda and the role of
the World Bank Group in advancing sound debt management and policy
frameworks, enhancing the accuracy and coverage of debt data, and
promoting the reconciliation of borrower and creditor accounts.

question: Was the external debt situation in 2025 identical between IDA-eligible countries and other developing economies?
answer: No, the external debt situation in 2025 was not identical. In IDA-eligible countries, external debt burdens declined slightly, with the debt-to-income ratio falling from 42.1 percent to 41.2 percent. In contrast, for other developing economies (specifically LMICs excluding China), the debt-to-income ratio rose to 34.5 percent as debt grew faster than national income [worldbank-idr-2026_p21_para_001].

Trends in External Debt, 2015–25
Renewed global inflationary pressures, geopolitical tensions, and decreased
fiscal space continued to put substantial pressure on the external debt positions
of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) in 2025. LMICs’ external
borrowing levels reached a record $9.4 trillion at the end of the year, increasing
5.5 percent from $8.9 trillion in 2024. LMIC external debt has grown about
60 percent over the past decade, and the 2025 increase was the largest since
the easing of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021.
